source_text: Hoc sentire et facere omnem servum dei oportet, etiam minoris loci, ut maioris fieri possit, si quem gradum in persecutionis tolerantia ascenderit. Sed cum ipsi auctores, id est ipsi diaconi et presbyteri et episcopi fugiunt, quomodo laicus intellegere poterit, qua ratione dictum: Fugite de civitate in civitatem? Itaque cum duces fugiunt, quis de gregario numero sustinebit ad gradum in acie figendum suadere? Certe quidem honus pastor animan pro pecoribus ponit, ut Moyses non domino adhuc Christo revelato et iam in se figurato ait: Si perdis hunc populum, inquit, et me pariter cum eo disperde. Ceterum Christo confirmante figuras suas ma(??)us pastor est qui viso lupo fugit et pecora diripienda derelinquit. Proicietur de villa pastor huiusmodi, detinebuntur illi missionis suae mercedes in compensationem, immo et de priore peculio eius exigetur detrimenti domini(??)i restitutio. Etenim qui habet, dabitur ei, ab eo autem, qui non habet, etiam quod videtur habere auferetur. Sic Zacharias comminatur: Ex(??)ge (??)homphaea in pastores et evellite oves, et superdueam m(??)num meam in pastores. In quos et Ezechiel et Hieremias iisdem minis perorant, quod non tantum de pecoribus improbe vescantur pascentes potius semetipses, verum et dispersum gregem faciant et in praedam esse omnibus bestiis agri, dum non est pastor illis. Quod numquam magis fit, quam cum in persecutione destituitur ecclesia a clero. Si et spiritum quis agnoverit, audiet fugitivos denotantem. Porro si eos qui gregi praesunt fugere, cum lupi irruunt, nec decet, immo nec licet (qui enim talem pastorem malum pronuntiavit, utique damnavit, omne autem quod damnatur, illicitum factum est sine dubio), ideo praepositos ecclesiae in persecutione fugere non oportebit. Ceterum si grex fugere deberet, non deberet praepositus gregis stare, sine causa staturus ad tutelam gregis, quam grex non desideraret, ex licentia fugae scilicet.
thought_title: Shepherds must not flee when the flock is attacked
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the duty of church leaders in persecution, arguing that if even the lowest servant must stand, then leaders who flee leave the flock without a shepherd.
pass_a_gloss: Every servant of God ought to feel this and do this, even one of lower rank, so that he may be able to become one of higher rank, if he has climbed any step in the endurance of persecution. But when the leaders themselves, that is the deacons themselves and presbyters and bishops, flee, how will a layman be able to understand by what reasoning it was said: Flee from city to city? And so when the leaders flee, who from the common number will hold out to persuade that a step must be fixed in the battle line? Certainly indeed the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, as Moses, when the Lord Christ had not yet been revealed and was already being prefigured in him, says: If you destroy this people, he says, destroy me also equally with it. But when Christ confirms his own figures, the bad shepherd is he who flees when he sees the wolf and abandons the sheep to be torn apart. A shepherd of this kind will be thrown out of the farm, the wages of his service will be withheld from him as compensation, indeed also from his former private property will be exacted restitution for the master's loss. For to him who has, it will be given, but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away. Thus Zechariah threatens: Draw a sword against the shepherds and pluck out the sheep, and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds. Against whom also Ezekiel and Jeremiah plead with the same threats, because they not only feed improperly on the sheep, pasturing rather themselves, but also make the flock scattered and a prey to all the beasts of the field, while there is no shepherd for them. This never happens more than when in persecution the church is abandoned by the clergy. If anyone has recognized the Spirit too, he will hear him marking out fugitives. Furthermore, if it is not fitting for those who are over the flock to flee when the wolves rush in, indeed it is not even permitted (for he who declared such a shepherd evil has certainly condemned him, but everything that is condemned has without doubt become unlawful), therefore it will not be right for those set over the church to flee in persecution. But if the flock ought to flee, the one set over the flock ought not to stand, since he would stand without cause for the protection of the flock, which the flock would not desire, because of the permission of flight, of course.

lemmas.gloss: to be fixed, to be planted

choices.why: The source reads 'honus' for 'bonus' (good), a common scribal error; the context of laying down life for the sheep confirms the sense.
The damaged word must be 'malus' (bad), contrasting with the good shepherd who lays down his life; the wolf and abandoned sheep confirm the sense.
The damaged word is 'dominici' (of the master), referring to the owner of the flock; the context of compensation and loss confirms this.
The damaged words are 'Exsurge' (arise) and 'rhomphaea' (sword), matching Zechariah's threat against shepherds; the context of threatening shepherds confirms the sense.
The damaged word is 'manum' (hand), completing the phrase 'I will bring my hand upon the shepherds' from Zechariah.

pass_b_english: Every servant of God ought to think and act this way, even one of lower rank, so that he may become greater if he climbs any step in enduring persecution. But when the leaders themselves—the deacons, presbyters, and bishops—flee, how can an ordinary believer understand why it was said, "Flee from city to city" (Matthew 10:23)? So when the commanders flee, who among the common soldiers will hold out to urge that a position be fixed in the battle line? Certainly the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, as Moses—before the Lord Christ was revealed, though already prefigured in him—says: "If you destroy this people," he says, "destroy me as well along with them" (Exodus 32:32). But Christ confirms his own figures: the bad shepherd is the one who sees the wolf and flees, leaving the sheep to be torn apart (John 10:12). Such a shepherd will be thrown out of the estate; the wages of his commission will be withheld as compensation, and restitution for the master's loss will be exacted even from his earlier property. For to the one who has, more will be given, but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away (Matthew 25:29). So Zechariah threatens: "Draw a sword against the shepherds and uproot the sheep, and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds" (Zechariah 13:7, paraphrased). Ezekiel and Jeremiah also speak at length against them with the same threats, because they not only feed improperly on the sheep, pasturing themselves rather than the flock, but also scatter the flock and make it prey for all the beasts of the field, since there is no shepherd for them (Ezekiel 34:2-5). This never happens more than when the church is abandoned by its clergy in persecution. If anyone recognizes the Spirit, he will hear the Spirit denouncing fugitives. Moreover, if those who are set over the flock flee when the wolves rush in, it is not fitting—indeed it is not even lawful. For the one who declared such a shepherd evil certainly condemned him, and everything that is condemned is without doubt made unlawful. Therefore the leaders of the church ought not to flee in persecution. But if the flock ought to flee, the leader of the flock ought not to stand, since he would stand to protect the flock to no purpose—a protection the flock would not want, given its license to flee.

problems.source_quote: Ex(??)ge (??)homphaea in pastores et evellite oves
problems.why: The source verb 'evellite' means 'pull up' or 'uproot', not 'scatter'. The English adds 'scatter' which is not in the source clause.
problems.fix: Draw a sword against the shepherds and uproot the sheep
problems.ruling: Source has 'evellite' (pull up/uproot) and no sword; English adds 'draw a sword' and uses 'scatter' altering meaning.
